questions.prompt: What is the key difference between an IAM user and an IAM role?

options.text: A user has long-term credentials; a role has no long-term credentials and is assumed for temporary ones
A role can only be used by the root user
A user is global and a role is Regional

questions.explanation: IAM users hold long-term credentials (passwords/access keys). Roles have no long-term credentials; a trusted principal assumes the role to get temporary credentials via STS.

questions.prompt: In IAM's evaluation logic, what happens when one policy allows an action and another explicitly denies it?

options.text: It depends on which was created first
The action is allowed only on weekends

questions.explanation: Access is denied by default; an explicit Allow grants it, but an explicit Deny anywhere overrides any Allow — deny always wins.

questions.prompt: Which are elements of an IAM policy statement? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A statement has Effect, Action, and Resource (plus optional Condition). IAM is global, so a policy statement has no Region element.

questions.prompt: How should an application running on an EC2 instance be given permission to read an S3 bucket?

options.text: Hardcode long-term access keys in the application
Attach an IAM role (instance profile) so it gets temporary credentials

questions.explanation: Attaching an IAM role to the instance gives the app temporary, automatically-rotated credentials, with no long-term secret to leak.

questions.prompt: Granting only the permissions actually needed and nothing more is the principle of least ____.
questions.explanation: Least privilege means granting the minimum permissions required, limiting the blast radius if credentials are misused.

questions.prompt: Match each IAM concept to its description.

pairs.right: An identity with long-term credentials for a person or app
A collection of users that share attached policies
An identity assumed for temporary credentials
A JSON document defining allowed or denied actions

questions.explanation: Users hold long-term credentials, groups bundle users for shared permissions, roles are assumed for temporary credentials, and policies are the JSON rules.
